newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian gasoline recovers but refiners not bullish.
newsitem.headline: Asian gasoline recovers but refiners not bullish.

text.p: SINGAPORE, Feb 3 (Singapore) - Gasoline prices in Asia have pulled out of the doldrums amid tight prompt supplies, but refiners are not bullish on the outlook and are not rushing to boost their output, industry sources said on Monday.

Singapore gasoline cargo prices have bucked the downward trend in products like diesel and fuel oil, which have been responsible for squeezing refiners' profits and forcing cuts in Singapore's refining by up to 130,000 barrels-per-day (bpd).
But for gasoline the picture has been different. In the last week, gasoline prices rose around $2.00 to more than $27.00 per barrel, widening the crack to about $4.70 from $3.00.
One of the region's main indicators, Taiwan's fixed price import tender for 95-octane unleaded reformate (gasoline), was awarded on Thursday at the highest level in some years, traders said.
"It is the highest ... we have never paid so high," a company official from state-owned Chinese Petroleum Corp (CPC) told Reuters. "We only awarded just one cargo because the number is not good."
CPC bought one cargo despite needing two, at $27.60 per barrel on a cost-and freight basis to Taiwan.
Last year, CPC bought around 30 cargoes of unleaded reformate at an average of around $22.00 per barrel, ranging $21.20 to $27.42.
"That is too aggressive," countered a western trader on the winning offer in the latest Taiwan tender. "There is more upside .. the market is still short."
Traders said February barrels in the region were already sold out and buyers were bidding up the market in search of cargoes.
But they said the demand was short term and would not support the market for long. Reforming margins therefore would remain under pressure.
While high domestic demand in the post-monsoon season has plugged Thai exports, refinery maintenance shutdowns in the Philippines, Sri Lanka and India have boosted demand.

India emerged to buy two to three gasoline cargoes a month for January and February, and four for March, a rise in the rate of its normal purchasing, which is 10-12 cargoes a year, Indian sources said.
A major said cargoes have been moving to India and the Middle East -- possibly for storage -- indicating the tightness of the market.

This is a drastic change from last year, when new refinery expansion, mainly in Thailand and South Korea, flooded Asia with gasoline by the middle of the year. But production cuts have helped to tighten the market.

Pockets of demand from the U.S., Australia and South Africa took out some of the surplus, but the glut of gasoline beared down on prices and refiners' profits from reforming, a secondary refining process that converts naphtha into reformate, a
blending component for gasoline, while producing hydrogen.
"In this region, that is Australia up to Japan, there is not that much new demand so it is basically long," said a trader at a Singapore refinery.

"At this moment, cuts (in Singapore reformer production) are around 75-80 percent as there are hydrogen constraints," said a refiner. Refiners require the hydrogen for other secondary refining process such as hydro desulphurisers and hydorcracking.

Yukong Ltd, the largest South Korean refiner shut down two reformers totalling 25,000-barrel-per-day January 24 for 10-15 days. A company source said it was better economics to sell the feedstock cargo instead of processing it.
"If margins are good, we can boost up production," said a refiner. "But (margins) are still below costs."
"If India buys 100,000 tonnes in the first half of the March, it could be quite tight," said one trader on the outlook. "But March should taper off from the high prompt levels."
--Singapore Newsroom (+65-870-3086)
